anatomy.intro: Chinlike rib notches and pale spine cushions stand out against the dark and green sectors of 'Black Widow'.

parts.function: The rib's chinlike steps shape the expandable water-storing body.
parts.label: Notched rib

parts.function: A pale cushion produces the small spine cluster.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: Short spines protect the surface around each areole.
parts.label: Curved spines

parts.function: Chlorophyll-bearing tissue contributes to the plant's photosynthesis.
parts.label: Green sector

flowers.text: The species bears pale green to brownish-yellow funnel-shaped flowers near the crown. Smooth buds lack the hairs and spines found on many other cactus flower buds.

growth.note: New growth broadens the crown; offsets gradually turn the original globe into a cluster.

stages.text: The young plant develops a compact ribbed body.
stages.title: Small globe

stages.text: New growth adds to the notched ribs at the top.
stages.title: Widening crown

stages.text: Mountain Crest reports regular offsets that can form a cluster.
stages.title: Offsetting cluster

habitat.text: The wild species comes from Paraguay and northeastern Argentina, including Chaco and Formosa. 'Black Widow' is a cultivated color form, so it has no separate wild habitat. Its smoky purple to nearly black body retains green tissue; the collection plant grows on its own roots rather than a graft.

lookalikes.name: Grafted moon cactus
lookalikes.text: Many vividly colored moon cacti lack enough chlorophyll and use a separate green rootstock. This own-root plant has a continuous base and green sectors.

mature.text: A compact ribbed globe can broaden into an offsetting cluster, with smaller heads gathered around the original stem.

nameStory.text: The species was first published as Echinocactus mihanovichii in 1905, then placed in Gymnocalycium in 1922.
